title: Seeing Structure in Expressions
short: Treat a chunk like (x + 1) or x² as a single quantity to rewrite an expression.
trouble: Students expand everything first instead of noticing that x⁴ − 9 is a difference of squares.

blocks.html: Good factoring starts with looking, not computing. In Factoring Completely you learned the patterns: common factors, trinomials, differences of squares. Here you learn to spot those patterns when they are wearing a disguise, by treating a whole chunk of an expression as one quantity.

If part of an expression repeats or is a perfect square, give it a single name, such as $u = x^2$ or $u = x + 1$. Factor the simpler expression in $u$, then put the chunk back. $x^4 - 9$ is $u^2 - 9$ with $u = x^2$, so it equals $(x^2 - 3)(x^2 + 3)$.

Algebra rules don't care what a letter stands for. The identity $u^2 - b^2 = (u - b)(u + b)$ is true when $u$ is a number, so it is true when $u$ is any expression that stands for a number, including $x^2$ or $(x + 1)$. Renaming a chunk just lets your eyes see a familiar shape.

blocks.title: A fourth power
steps: $x^2 - 4$ is again a difference of squares: $(x - 2)(x + 2)$. The sum $x^2 + 4$ does not factor over the real numbers.

blocks.title: A shifted square
steps: Check by expanding both: $(x + 2)^2 - 25 = x^2 + 4x - 21$ and $(x - 3)(x + 7) = x^2 + 4x - 21$.

blocks.name: graph
blocks.cap: $f(x) = (x + 2)^2 - 25$ and its factored form $g(x) = (x - 3)(x + 7)$ (dashed) draw the same parabola. The factored form shows the zeros, 3 and $-7$, at a glance.

blocks.html: Expanding everything first. Turning $(x + 2)^2 - 25$ into $x^2 + 4x - 21$ works, but it hides the pattern and gives you a harder trinomial to factor. With $x^4 - 9$, expanding doesn't even help. Look for squares (and other repeated chunks) before you multiply anything out.
